Notes: Earliest documented Jewish presence (basis of Year Established): Josephus, War 7.8.3, 'Upon this top of the hill, Jonathan the high priest first of all built a fortress, and called it Masada' - a Hasmonean (Judean) royal fortress. 'Jonathan' is identified either with Jonathan Apphus (152-143 BCE) or, more usually, with Alexander Jannaeus (103-76 BCE); year = midpoint of the Hasmonean period (140-37 BCE) = -90, c. A garrison stronghold, not a civilian settlement; no number given.

Archaeological evidence of the Hasmonean phase: Hasmonean-period pottery, about a dozen Ptolemaic coins and dozens of coins of Alexander Jannaeus (103-76 BCE) were found; no Hasmonean building remains survive apart from two cisterns that may have been hewn then. Suggests a small Hasmonean (Jewish) garrison presence; c. midpoint of Hasmonean period. (Hebrew Wikipedia used as last resort.)

Josephus, War 1.12.1: after the death of Malichus (43 BCE), Malichus's brother seized many fortresses in Judea, 'and among them the strongest of them all, Masada' - Masada held by a Judean faction's garrison; c. 43/42 BCE. Garrison, no residents counted.

Josephus, War 1.13.8: fleeing the Parthians and Antigonus (40 BCE), Herod reached the fortress 'with his nearest relations' (incl. his Hasmonean betrothed Mariamme and her mother) and 'left eight hundred of his men as a guard for the women' with provisions for a siege. The 800 is a guard/garrison figure, not resident population (Notes only); Josephus also says the fortress could not hold the more than 9,000 people who had gathered around Herod.

Josephus, Antiquities 14.15.1-4: Antigonus besieged 'those that were in Masada', short of water; Herod's brother Joseph planned to flee to the Arabians 'with two hundred of his own friends' until rain filled the reservoirs; Herod then 'easily recovered his relations again that were in Masada' (39 BCE). The 200 is a subset (Joseph's companions), Notes only.

Herod the Great built the fortress-palace of Masada between 37 and 31 BCE as a refuge for himself (year = midpoint, c.). The hall later used as the rebels' synagogue was part of the Herodian construction. Royal fortress with garrison/staff; no figure for Jewish residents.

Josephus, War 2.17.2: at the outbreak of the revolt (66 CE) rebels 'took it by treachery, and slew the Romans that were there, and put others of their own party to keep it' - start of the Jewish rebel occupation of Masada (66-73/74 CE). No number.

Josephus, War 2.17.9: after the murder of Menahem in Jerusalem (autumn 66 CE) 'A few there were of them who privately escaped to Masada, among whom was Eleazar, the son of Jairus', who afterwards 'acted the part of a tyrant at Masada'. Named individual (Eleazar ben Yair) resident from 66 CE; 'a few' refugees.

Josephus, War 4.7.2: the Sicarii who held Masada raided Engaddi (Ein Gedi) at Passover (c. 68 CE), killed 'above seven hundred' women and children there and brought the plunder into Masada; 'there came to them every day, from all parts, not a few men as corrupt as themselves' - growing rebel population at Masada. The 700 are Ein Gedi casualties, not Masada residents (Notes only).

Ehud Netzer (BAS, 'The Last Days and Hours at Masada'): the Zealots occupied Masada from 66 CE ('During their seven years of residence on the mountain'); private residences were divided into secondary units; the western palace, 'too large for one family', was the residence of a group living collectively; Netzer notes women, children and the elderly could have carried earth for the last-ditch wall. Year = c. midpoint of the 66-73/74 occupation. Organized community of families; Netzer gives no count. (PDF text extracted locally.)

Rebel-period community features (Hebrew Wikipedia): the casemate wall served as housing for the defenders; rooms of the small palaces were converted into dwellings for families; mud and stone shelters built; the Herodian hall was converted into a synagogue during the Great Revolt; two public miqvaot (north and south, the southern one in casemate 1197) and many purification basins; dozens of revolt coins; ostraca 'ma'aser kohen' (priestly tithe) and the name Hezekiah. In 70 CE further Sicarii and their families expelled from Jerusalem joined. c. 70 CE; no count.

Lawrence H. Schiffman (Reclaiming the Dead Sea Scrolls, 1994): Masada captured by rebels in 66 CE; two ritual baths of the period built 'in the manner prescribed by later rabbinic halakhah'; synagogue facing Jerusalem; parts of fifteen biblical and apocryphal scrolls (incl. Ben Sira, Jubilees, Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice), some hidden in pits under the synagogue floor and in casemate rooms; ostracon on priestly tithes. Evidence of an observant Jewish community; c. 70 CE; no count.

New Encyclopedia of Archaeological Excavations in the Holy Land (Masada entry): 'Zealots constructed ritual bath 1301' NW of the cistern; tiny residential structures with many First Revolt finds; ostraca in square 174 possibly where 'the communal life of the rebels was administered'; a coin group dated 73/74 CE marks the end of the revolt occupation. c. 70 CE; no count.

Encyclopedia of the Bible (Masada): at the start of the war Masada was taken by Zealots; 'A synagogue and some ritual baths also were found', 'several hundreds ostraca inscribed in Heb. and Aram.', scroll fragments of Genesis, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Ezekiel and Psalms. Literate, observant Jewish community; c. 70 CE.

BMCR review of J. Magness, Masada: From Jewish Revolt to Modern Myth (2019): rebel occupation 66-74 CE by 'a fluid population composed indeed of Sicarii but also of some Essenes'; sectarian scrolls 'attest to a small Essene community'; housing, synagogue, miqva'ot, stone and dung vessels reflect purity concerns and the rebels' poverty; women present. c. 70 CE; no count.

T. Liberman and E. Regev, 'Masada's Rebels: Elitism, Feasts and Social Structure in Light of the Pottery' (Cathedra 178, 2021; abstract): the rich ceramic assemblage indicates an economically strong society; in Building 13 and the casemate dwellings each small unit cooked separately while other buildings dined communally - 'distinct, perhaps opposing, groups of residents'. Household-based community; c. 70 CE; no count in abstract.

Tel Aviv University 2017 excavation (G. Stiebel): Area A 'bore the remnants of the First Jewish Revolt era refugee camp' within Herod's ruins; after its capture by Sicarii under Menahem, Masada became 'a place of refuge for other Jewish populations, including Essenes' (and Samaritans). c. 70 CE; no count.

Josephus, War 7.8.1: Flavius Silva marched against Masada, held by the Sicarii under 'one Eleazar, a potent man, and the commander of these Sicarii, that had seized upon it', a descendant of Judas the Galilean. Start of the Roman siege (73 or 73/74 CE). No number.

Josephus, War 7.9.1: mass death of the defenders on 15 Xanthicus (Nisan), 73 or (per Eck/Cotton dating) 74 CE: 'Those others were nine hundred and sixty in number, the women and children being withal included in that computation'; two women and five children hid and survived (967 in all). Ancient figure = death toll of the besieged rebel community (men, women, children); per the rules kept in Notes, Population blank. Excavations found remains of at most 28 people; scholars debate the figure.

Jewish Virtual Library: the Romans breached the wall 'in the spring of 74 CE'; the defenders were 'almost one thousand men, women and children' (restating Josephus' 967; Notes only, Population blank); remains of three skeletons of a man, a woman and a child found in the northern palace; revolt shekels of all years of the Revolt found.

Archaeological remains of the defenders (HNN, summarising N. Ben-Yehuda and others): Yadin's excavations 'uncovered the remains of only 28 people' - 3 under the northern palace debris and 25 in a cave below the southern cliff; Josephus' figure is 967; 'The whereabouts of the remaining 932 bodies remains a mystery'. Skeletal count, not population (Notes only).

End of Jewish presence: after the fall (73/74 CE) and the death of the rebel community (War 7.9.1), Josephus, War 7.10.1: 'the general left a garrison in the fortress to keep it, and he himself went away to Cesarea'; 'there were now no enemies left in the country'. Population 0 = the Jewish rebel community destroyed and the site held by a Roman garrison.
